case_study_insert.main_stem: Quarry Ridge Materials (QRM) is a private limited company in the quarried aggregates sector, employing a workforce of 50 at its limestone extraction site. Founded in 2011 by Niamh Ridge, the business supplies crushed limestone to regional construction contractors and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. QRM plans to invest $920,000 in a mobile crushing and screening plant with dust-suppression technology, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $320,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.50 a unit and a selling price of $14.50, and currently produces 100,000 units a year. QRM faces two operational problems: dust-related absenteeism has reached 8% and stone-dust complaints from nearby residents are rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q4 2025: The crushing line produced 25,000 units last quarter at a defect rate of 2.4%, down from 3.8% a year ago. Customer complaints about stone dust fell from 31 to 14 per month. Average delivery lead time is 4.1 days. A survey of 450 construction customers found that 61% would pay up to $0.50 more per unit for low-dust eco-aggregate made with recycled stone fines, and 48% require suppliers to meet dust-emission standards. Training records show 18 of the 50 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new screens; off-the-job certification courses at the technical college cost $950 per employee. The plant manager is comparing end-of-line quality control inspection with quality assurance based on prevention and team working.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Quarry Ridge Materials for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Construction Bulletin (January 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $13.00 to $13.75 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills at extraction sites. (3) Diesel and wear-part input costs have risen 9.6% year-on-year, while construction cost inflation is running at 6.2% and infrastructure spending grew 2.9% over the same period.

questions.question_text: QRM is funding part of its $920,000 crushing plant with a $600,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for QRM of using retained profit for the $320,000 portion instead of borrowing more.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using retained profit for the $320,000 portion means QRM pays no interest or capital repayments on that money, which protects its cash flow while it already carries fixed costs of $360,000 a year and a $600,000 ten-year bank loan. The saving can be spent on dust-suppression technology and on replacing screens, so the flat-structure quarry can tackle dust-related absenteeism of 8% without adding another fixed commitment. Every dollar of interest avoided also supports the $6.00 contribution per unit on each of the 100,000 units it produces.

Point 2: Retained profit does not require collateral or a charge over QRM's quarry assets, so Niamh Ridge's private limited company keeps control of the mobile crushing and screening plant without a lender able to repossess it if construction contractors cut orders. It is also faster and more flexible than arranging additional debt: the $320,000 is already in the business and can be released as the plant is commissioned, whereas a new loan would need approval and would raise the risk that the 48% of customers demanding dust-emission standards are not served on time.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over borrowing identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation linked to QRM's $320,000 funding, its $600,000 loan and its quarry operations.

questions.question_text: QRM is promoting its new low-dust eco-aggregate to construction contractors. Consider advertising in construction trade journals, a programme of free site demonstrations, or paid social-media campaigns. Which should QRM choose to win new customers? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Trade journal advertising: A trade journal would put QRM's low-dust eco-aggregate in front of the regional construction contractors it already supplies, and printed technical specifications suit a product where 48% of surveyed customers require dust-emission standards. It is relatively cheap for a 50-employee quarry, but readership is slow to convert and many readers are outside QRM's delivery radius; it also cannot demonstrate the dust-suppression plant actually working, which is the product's main selling point.

Free site demonstrations: Inviting contractors to the quarry lets them see the mobile crushing and screening plant and verify dust levels for themselves, directly addressing the 31 dust complaints a month that the report records. Technical staff can explain the recycled stone fines and close orders on site. The drawbacks are high staff time, travel costs for customers and limited reach: only a small number of the 450 surveyed construction customers could attend, so this cannot by itself fill the extra capacity of the $920,000 investment.

Paid social-media campaigns: Targeted posts can reach exactly the contractors who check dust-emission standards, show short videos of the suppression technology and generate measurable enquiries at low cost, complementing the 61% of respondents who would pay $0.50 more. However, social media is easily ignored in a busy feed, needs constant content, and does not give the technical reassurance a quarry product requires.

Recommendation: QRM should choose a programme of free site demonstrations, supported by low-cost social-media follow-up. Demonstrations are rejected by neither cost nor scale because they convert the 48% standards-driven buyers fastest and directly counter the dust complaints; trade journals are rejected as passive and untargeted, while social media alone is rejected because it lacks the physical proof that makes the $920,000 dust-suppression investment credible.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the promotional options with limited reference to QRM's product or customers.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of QRM's quarry and survey evidence.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in context and gives a justified recommendation that explains why trade journals and social media are rejected.

questions.question_text: QRM's dust-related absenteeism has reached 8%. Explain two benefits for QRM of using democratic leadership to motivate its extraction and crushing team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the 50 quarry workers to contribute ideas on how the mobile crushing and screening plant should be run, which helps satisfy esteem and social needs and raises job satisfaction. Operators who help set sieve-changing routines and dust-control practices are more likely to attend regularly, so the practice attacks the 8% dust-related absenteeism directly. It also fits QRM's flat organisational structure, where short communication channels let a suggestion from the screening line reach Niamh Ridge quickly rather than passing through several management layers.

Point 2: Consulting the team produces practical improvements that a manager away from the face may miss, such as better positioning of dust-suppression nozzles, helping the line hold its 2.4% defect rate and reduce the 31 monthly dust complaints. Higher involvement builds commitment and lowers labour turnover, protecting the 25,000 units produced each quarter and avoiding the $950 per employee cost of off-the-job certification for replacements. In a private limited company funding a $920,000 plant with a $600,000 loan, keeping experienced operators is cheaper than repeatedly recruiting and retraining them.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of democratic leadership identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for applied analysis of QRM's absenteeism, flat structure, defect rate and training costs.

questions.question_text: QRM must reduce dust exposure around its new dust-suppression plant. Consider on-the-job training on the screens or off-the-job certification at the technical college. Which should QRM choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching the 18 untrained staff beside the actual screens teaches the exact dust-control routines QRM needs, costs no course fees and keeps those workers producing during the 25,000-unit quarter. It allows immediate correction by experienced operators and reinforces the team working needed to cut the 31 monthly dust complaints. Its weaknesses are that trainers are themselves production staff whose output suffers, that bad habits can spread, and that there is no external certificate for the 48% of customers who want evidence of dust-emission standards.

Off-the-job certification: The technical college course at $950 per employee would cost $17,100 for all 18 staff, a small fraction of the $920,000 investment, and gives a recognised qualification that supports QRM's claim to meet dust-emission standards. It removes 18 people from a workforce of 50 for the course period, however, risking output and raising dust-related pressure on those left behind while absenteeism is already 8%; the generic syllabus may also need site-specific follow-up.

Decision: QRM should choose on-the-job training first, followed by short college certification for a smaller group of senior operators. On-the-job training is rejected as a complete answer only because it lacks formal evidence, but it wins on cost, machine relevance and uninterrupted output; full off-the-job training is rejected now because losing 18 of 50 workers and spending $17,100 while dust absenteeism is 8% would disrupt the crushing line when QRM most needs steady output. A mixed approach also spreads the risk if college places are limited, and part of the fee can be reserved for the 48% of customers who want evidence of dust-emission standards.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training methods with minimal application to QRM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses benefits and drawbacks of both methods using QRM's figures, with limited judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Fully evaluates both methods in QRM's context and reaches a justified decision that rejects the alternative.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how QRM's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $360,000 ÷ ($14.50 − $8.50) = $360,000 ÷ $6.00 = 60,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 60,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $14.50 − $8.50 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways QRM's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 60,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 100,000 units: the margin of safety is 40,000 units, so QRM can judge how far crushed-limestone demand could fall before the $920,000 crushing plant stops covering its $360,000 fixed costs.
2. Use the $6.00 contribution per unit to model price decisions, for example a $0.50 discount to $14.00 would leave $5.50 contribution, showing managers how much extra volume is needed before offering regional contractors a lower price.
3. Set output and repayment targets: at 100,000 units the total contribution is 100,000 × $6.00 = $600,000, enough to cover the $360,000 fixed costs and leave $240,000 towards the $600,000 bank loan interest, so the finance plan can be checked before further capital is committed.
4. Benchmark unit costs with average total cost of $12.10 ($360,000 ÷ 100,000 + $8.50) and labour productivity of 100,000 ÷ 50 = 2,000 units per worker, so management can see whether the 8% dust-related absenteeism or the 2.4% defect rate is pushing costs above that benchmark.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 60,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 40,000-unit margin of safety against 100,000-unit output; pricing/discount modelling from $6.00 contribution; loan-feasibility target of $600,000 total contribution; and unit-cost benchmarking at $12.10 with 2,000 units per worker.

working_marks: 1 mark for the correct formula and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in each of (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each of four valid applied uses in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate QRM's profitability by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has QRM's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 42.5%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 12.5%
ROCE 2024 = 14.0%
ROCE 2025 = 16.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit = $1,400,000 revenue − $840,000 cost of sales = $560,000; 2025 gross profit = $1,600,000 − $920,000 = $680,000. For 2024, $560,000 ÷ $1,400,000 = 0.400; $168,000 operating profit ÷ $1,400,000 = 0.120; $168,000 ÷ $1,200,000 capital employed = 0.140. For 2025, $680,000 ÷ $1,600,000 = 0.425; $200,000 ÷ $1,600,000 = 0.125; $200,000 ÷ $1,250,000 = 0.160.

Evaluation: Revenue grew by ($1,600,000 − $1,400,000) ÷ $1,400,000 = 14.3%, while gross profit grew from $560,000 to $680,000, so the business kept more of each sales dollar after direct costs. The margin on sales improved because cost of sales rose by only $80,000 against a $200,000 rise in revenue, suggesting better control of quarrying and haulage costs despite the reported diesel and wear-part pressures. Operating profit rose from $168,000 to $200,000, a faster increase than revenue, so overheads were also absorbed more effectively. ROCE improved even though capital employed increased from $1,200,000 to $1,250,000 to fund the new plant, which is a favourable sign for the owners. Interest payable edged up from $28,000 to $32,000, so the $600,000 loan does reduce the profit left for the private limited company's shareholders, but the effect is small beside the $200,000 operating profit.

Conclusion: QRM's profitability has improved. All three measures moved favourably — gross margin 40.0% to 42.5%, operating margin 12.0% to 12.5% and ROCE 14.0% to 16.0% — and the ROCE gain was achieved while the asset base grew, so the $920,000 investment is already supporting stronger returns rather than diluting them.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Quotes figures from Appendix 2 with little or no accurate calculation.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates the three ratios for both years and describes the trend with some reference to QRM.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for all three ratios in both years plus detailed evaluation of revenue, costs, capital employed and interest, ending in a justified conclusion.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for QRM of producing low-dust eco-aggregate made with recycled stone fines.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 450 construction customers found that 61% would pay up to $0.50 more per unit for low-dust eco-aggregate and that 48% already require suppliers to meet dust-emission standards. That premium would lift selling price from $14.50 to $15.00 and, with the $8.50 variable cost unchanged, raise contribution per unit from $6.00 to $6.50 — about $65,000 a year on 100,000 units. It also gives QRM a defensible reason to win listings with the contractors whose dust complaints have reached 31 a month.

Disadvantage: Recycling stone fines into the product adds handling and screening work that could raise the $8.50 variable cost, so the $0.50 premium might be wholly absorbed and the 42.5% gross margin in Appendix 2 would slip back. If the recycled fines vary in quality, the line's 2.4% defect rate could rise and more output would be scrapped, while dust-related absenteeism of 8% would still need the $920,000 dust-suppression plant to deliver savings before the eco-aggregate can be sold at a genuine premium.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for development using QRM's survey data, price, variable cost, defect rate and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in diesel and wear-part costs will affect QRM. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): If QRM's $600,000 ten-year bank loan is on a variable rate, the increase of 0.75 percentage points adds 0.0075 × $600,000 = $4,500 a year, which is small against fixed costs of $360,000 and operating profit of $200,000. If the loan is fixed, the direct cost is zero. Higher rates may also make future borrowing for the $920,000 programme dearer, but QRM can reduce this risk by fixing the rate, so the effect is limited and manageable.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, from $13.00 to $13.75 an hour): With a workforce of 50, a wage rise feeds into quarrying and screening labour costs and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual wage total can be calculated honestly. The defensible comparison is with the productivity the data do support: 100,000 units ÷ 50 workers = 2,000 units per worker. If that holds, the higher wage per hour is spread over 2,000 units each; if dust-related absenteeism of 8% pulls output down, unit labour cost rises and the $6.00 contribution per unit is squeezed. This is a real but controllable pressure.

Input-cost inflation (9.6% on diesel and wear parts): The insert states variable cost of $8.50 per unit but does not decompose it, so the only honest bound is to assume the whole variable cost is exposed: 9.6% × $8.50 = about $0.82 per unit, and at 100,000 units that is roughly $81,600 a year (100,000 × $0.816). Even a smaller exposed share would cut contribution materially below $6.00, and higher diesel costs also affect deliveries to the 450 surveyed customers. QRM can recover at most part of this through the $0.50 eco-aggregate premium found in the research.

Conclusion: The 9.6% rise in diesel and wear-part costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every unit produced, can erode around $81,600 of contribution on the stated bound, and directly undermines the return on the $920,000 plant. The interest rise adds only $4,500 a year and can be fixed, while the wage rise can be offset by maintaining 2,000 units per worker, so neither matches the scale or persistence of input-cost inflation.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Lists the three external changes with little application to QRM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses at least two changes with correct use of QRM's figures and some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three changes in QRM's context, uses only insert-derived arithmetic and reaches a justified greatest-impact conclusion.
